original_value:
The bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) is crucial for modeling the appearance of real-world materials. In production rendering, analytic BRDF models are often used to approximate the surface appearance since they are compact and flexible. Measured BRDFs usually have a more realistic appearance, but consume much more storage and are hard to modify. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for connecting measured and analytic BRDFs. First, we develop a robust method for separating a measured BRDF into diffuse and specular components. This is commonly done in analytic models, but has been difficult previously to do explicitly for measured BRDFs. This diffuse-specular separation allows novel measured BRDF editing on the diffuse and specular parts separately. In addition, we conduct analysis on each part of the measured BRDF, and demonstrate a more intuitive and lower-dimensional PCA model than Nielsen
            et al.
            [2015]. In fact, our measured BRDF model has the same number of parameters (8 parameters) as the commonly used analytic models, such as the GGX model. Finally, we visualize the analytic and measured BRDFs in the same space, and directly demonstrate their similarities and differences. We also design an analytic fitting algorithm for two-lobe materials, which is more robust, efficient and simple, compared to previous non-convex optimization-based analytic fitting methods.

result.paraphrase: The bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) is essential for modeling how real-world materials look. In production rendering, analytic BRDF models are commonly used to approximate surface appearance because they are compact and flexible. Measured BRDFs tend to look more realistic, but they require far more storage and are harder to edit. In this paper, we present a new framework that links measured and analytic BRDFs. We first introduce a robust approach for splitting a measured BRDF into diffuse and specular components. While this is standard in analytic models, it has previously been difficult to do explicitly for measured BRDFs. This diffuse-specular decomposition enables new editing of measured BRDFs by adjusting the diffuse and specular parts independently. We also analyze each component of the measured BRDF and show a more intuitive, lower-dimensional PCA model than Nielsen et al. [2015]. In fact, our measured BRDF model uses the same number of parameters, 8, as widely used analytic models such as GGX. Finally, we place analytic and measured BRDFs in the same space to directly illustrate their similarities and differences. We also develop an analytic fitting algorithm for two-lobe materials that is more robust, efficient, and simple than prior methods based on non-convex optimization.
